quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Many teenagers stay up late on their phones and then struggle to wake up for school. Sleep experts suggest a simple habit: leave the phone in another room an hour before bed. Students who tried this said they fell asleep faster and felt less tired the next day.
quests.question: What is the main subject of this text about teenagers and phones?
options: A habit that helps teenagers sleep
Why teenagers dislike getting up for school
A ban on phones in classrooms
quests.correctAnswer: A habit that helps teenagers sleep
quests.hint: Test each option against the whole passage, not just the opening sentence.
quests.explanation: The passage describes a problem, offers one habit, and reports its results, so the habit is the main idea. School dislike and phone bans are never discussed.

quests.instruction: Read the text quickly and answer the question.
quests.passage: A small wooden box outside Grace's house holds about thirty books that neighbours can take for free. Anyone is welcome to leave books too, and the box is rarely empty. Grace built it last spring after noticing how many novels were gathering dust on her own shelves.
quests.question: Why did Grace build the box?
options: The local library had closed down recently
She wanted to sell her old books online
She owned many books she no longer read
Her neighbours asked her to start one
quests.correctAnswer: She owned many books she no longer read
quests.hint: The reason is tied to something Grace observed. Find the phrase that introduces it.
quests.explanation: Novels "gathering dust" means unread books, which is what led to the idea. Nobody asked her, and the books are free, so selling is not the motive.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: The city has added twelve kilometres of protected bike lanes this year. Officials say cycling has risen by a quarter since the first lanes opened, and fewer accidents have been reported on those streets. Some drivers complain that parking has become harder, but most residents support the project.
quests.question: Which detail best shows that the bike lanes are working?
options: More people cycle and there are fewer accidents
Twelve kilometres of new lanes were built this year
quests.correctAnswer: More people cycle and there are fewer accidents
quests.hint: Decide what would count as evidence of results, rather than facts about the project.
quests.explanation: Increased cycling and fewer accidents are outcomes. Distance built describes the work, and opinions show support, not effectiveness.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Fair-trade coffee guarantees farmers a minimum price, even when world prices fall. Buyers also pay an extra amount that the farming community can spend on schools or clean water. Critics say the system is costly to join, but many small growers say the stable income is worth it.
quests.question: What is the writer's main point about fair-trade coffee?
options: It gives small farmers a more secure income
It makes coffee much cheaper for supermarket shoppers
quests.correctAnswer: It gives small farmers a more secure income
quests.hint: Notice how the passage ends. Growers' opinion often tells you where the writer stands.
quests.explanation: A guaranteed minimum price and community payments add up to security. The costs mentioned are a criticism, not the main point.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Children who grow up speaking two languages often switch between them without effort. Researchers have found that they can also be better at ignoring distractions and shifting attention from one task to another. However, being bilingual does not automatically make a child cleverer.
quests.question: According to the passage, what can bilingual children do well?
options: Learn a third language much faster
quests.correctAnswer: Concentrate despite distractions
quests.hint: The benefit is mentioned in the middle. The last sentence warns against overstating it.
quests.explanation: Ignoring distractions is a stated strength. "Cleverer" is exactly what the final sentence says is not automatic.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: On the last Friday of each month, the city museum stays open until ten in the evening. Tickets are half price after six, and there is live music in the main hall. The first Friday drew three hundred visitors; last month, more than a thousand came.
quests.question: What does the last sentence mainly show?
options: Tickets are now too expensive for most families
Evening openings have become much more popular
The main hall is too small
quests.correctAnswer: Evening openings have become much more popular
quests.hint: Compare the two numbers in the last sentence and ask what changed.
quests.explanation: Three hundred grew to over a thousand, which shows rising popularity. The passage never mentions price complaints or crowding.

quests.instruction: Read the text quickly and answer the question.
quests.passage: A new app tells bus riders exactly where their bus is. Before it launched, passengers often waited at cold stops without knowing whether a bus had already gone. Now they can see its position on a map and leave home at the right moment, which many say has made their mornings calmer.
quests.question: Which headline would best suit this article about the bus app?
options: An App That Ends the Waiting Game
Ten Tips for Calmer School Mornings
quests.correctAnswer: An App That Ends the Waiting Game
quests.hint: A good title covers the whole text, not one small detail.
quests.explanation: Every sentence concerns what the app does for waiting passengers. "Calmer mornings" is only one result, so it is too narrow for a title.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: On hot days, streets with many trees can be up to five degrees cooler than streets without them. The leaves provide shade, and they also release water vapour that cools the air. Because of this, several cities have begun planting trees along roads where people wait for buses.
quests.question: Why are cities planting trees near bus stops?
options: To reduce traffic noise near the stops
To cool the places where people wait
quests.correctAnswer: To cool the places where people wait
quests.hint: The word "because" points backward to the cause and forward to the action.
quests.explanation: Trees cool the air, so planting them where people wait makes sense. Noise, safety and rainwater are not mentioned.

quests.instruction: Read the text quickly and answer the question.
quests.passage: Two former classmates started a company that delivers home-cooked lunches from retired neighbours to office workers. Each cook chooses the weekly menu and keeps most of the money from every meal. The founders say the idea began when one of them realised her grandmother missed cooking for other people.
quests.question: What gave the founders the idea?
options: Noticing that an older relative missed cooking
Seeing that retired people needed cheap groceries
Hearing that offices had no canteens
quests.correctAnswer: Noticing that an older relative missed cooking
quests.hint: The origin of the idea is usually placed near the end of a company story.
quests.explanation: The final sentence names the grandmother as the starting point. The other choices sound reasonable but are not in the text.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: At Pine Hill Primary, every class has a small vegetable bed. Children plant seeds in spring, water them each week, and harvest in autumn. The school kitchen then uses the vegetables in lunches. Teachers say pupils who grow their own food are more willing to try new dishes.
quests.question: What is the central message of the story from Pine Hill Primary?
options: Primary schools need much bigger kitchens and gardens
A school garden changes how children approach food
quests.correctAnswer: A school garden changes how children approach food
quests.hint: Ask what the teachers' comment at the end says about the whole project.
quests.explanation: The activities lead up to the teachers' observation about trying new dishes. Seasons and kitchens are details of how the project works.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Bella's Ice Cream changes its flavours with the seasons. In summer it sells peach and mint; in autumn, pumpkin and cinnamon. Regular customers often ask for a flavour to return, so the owner keeps a list of requests on the shop wall. The most requested flavour last winter was ginger.
quests.question: How does the owner keep track of what customers want?
options: She writes requests on a list
She asks the staff to remember them all
quests.correctAnswer: She writes requests on a list
quests.hint: One sentence describes a method. Skip the flavour names.
quests.explanation: The list on the wall is the method. Flavours and seasons are interesting but answer a different question.

quests.instruction: Read the text quickly and answer the question.
quests.passage: A recent study of secondary students found that up to two hours of homework a night can improve results. Beyond that, extra time brought no further benefit, and students who worked very late often slept badly. The researchers suggest teachers set shorter, clearer tasks instead of more of them.
quests.question: What do the researchers recommend?
options: Two extra hours of study each night
A later start to the school day
quests.correctAnswer: Fewer but clearer homework tasks
quests.hint: A recommendation often begins with a verb like "suggest" or "advise".
quests.explanation: The last sentence gives the advice. Two hours is the point after which benefits stop, so the first option misreads it.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Flooding is one of the most common natural disasters, and many deaths occur when people drive through flooded roads. Just thirty centimetres of moving water can lift a small car. Authorities therefore urge drivers to turn around and find another route, however urgent their journey feels.
quests.question: What is the main message of the passage?
options: Drivers should never enter flooded roads
Small cars are unsafe on every kind of road
quests.correctAnswer: Drivers should never enter flooded roads
quests.hint: Look for the sentence that tells people what to do, then check it covers the rest.
quests.explanation: The facts about danger all support the final instruction to turn around. Frequency of floods is only implied by "most common."

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: In many rural areas, fire brigades depend on volunteers who have other jobs. When the alarm sounds, a farmer or teacher may leave work and be at the station within minutes. Recruiting is becoming harder, since younger people often move to cities and training takes many evenings.
quests.question: Why is it getting harder to find volunteers?
options: The stations are too far from most villages
Young people leave and training takes time
quests.correctAnswer: Young people leave and training takes time
quests.hint: A reason with "since" often holds two linked causes.
quests.explanation: Two causes follow "since": young people moving away and the long training. Pay is never mentioned.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Language apps often reward users with a streak, a counter of consecutive days of practice. Many learners find it motivating, but some feel anxious about breaking the chain. Teachers suggest that steady progress matters more than a perfect record, and that a missed day is not a failure.
quests.question: What is the teachers' view?
options: Streaks are essential to all language learning
Steady progress beats a perfect record
quests.correctAnswer: Steady progress beats a perfect record
quests.hint: Separate what learners feel from what teachers say.
quests.explanation: Teachers place steady progress above a perfect record. The anxiety belongs to some learners, not to the teachers.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: More companies now let employees work from home two or three days a week. Workers save commuting time and often report better concentration. However, some managers worry that new staff learn more slowly when they cannot watch colleagues at work, so many firms ask newcomers to come to the office more often.
quests.question: What overall topic connects the points about working from home?
options: How to design a home office
Which kinds of jobs cannot be done from home at all
Benefits and worries of part-time home working
quests.correctAnswer: Benefits and worries of part-time home working
quests.hint: A contrast word splits a passage into two sides. Both sides belong to the main idea.
quests.explanation: The first half gives benefits and "however" introduces a worry, so the passage weighs both. Office design and job types never appear.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: One supermarket chain now sells slightly bruised fruit at a reduced price instead of throwing it away. It also donates unsold bread each evening to local shelters. The company estimates these steps have cut its food waste by nearly a third in two years.
quests.question: What happens to the unsold bread?
options: It is sold cheaper the next day
quests.correctAnswer: It is given to shelters
quests.hint: The fruit and the bread are treated differently. Keep them separate.
quests.explanation: Bruised fruit is discounted, but unsold bread is donated to shelters. Mixing the two products leads to the wrong option.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: A school in a sunny region has covered its roof with solar panels. The panels produce more electricity than the building needs, so the extra is sold to the local grid. The money pays for new science equipment. Students also use the panels' data in their maths lessons.
quests.question: Which title best reflects the story of the school's roof?
options: A School That Profits from the Sun
quests.correctAnswer: A School That Profits from the Sun
quests.hint: Choose the title that covers electricity, money and lessons together.
quests.explanation: The panels produce power, earn money and support learning, so "profits from the sun" covers all of it. The other titles pick up only side details.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Every year, millions of old mobile phones end up in drawers instead of recycling bins. They contain small amounts of gold, copper and other useful metals that can be recovered and reused. Some shops now pay customers a small sum for old phones, hoping to persuade more people to hand them in.
quests.question: What is the main idea?
options: Phones should be built to last much longer than now
Old phones contain valuable metals worth recycling
quests.correctAnswer: Old phones contain valuable metals worth recycling
quests.hint: Ask what the shops' offer is trying to achieve, then link it to the first sentence.
quests.explanation: The passage starts with the problem, explains why it matters, and ends with a way to solve it. That chain points to recycling.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Beginners preparing for a ten-kilometre race are usually advised to train three times a week for eight weeks. Two runs should be short and easy, and the third gradually longer. A rest day between runs is essential, because muscles get stronger during recovery, not during the run itself.
quests.question: Why are rest days important?
options: Races are usually held on the rest days
quests.correctAnswer: Muscles get stronger while recovering
quests.hint: The explanation comes after the word "because."
quests.explanation: The final sentence says strength is built during recovery. This detail explains the earlier advice about rest.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Residents of Oak Lane started a neighbourhood group after several bicycles were stolen. Members share news in a chat group and agree to notice unusual activity. Since it began in January, no more bikes have been taken, and the group has also organised a summer street party.
quests.question: What has changed since the group began?
options: Fewer families now live on Oak Lane
No more bicycles have been stolen
quests.correctAnswer: No more bicycles have been stolen
quests.hint: Look for a result attached to a starting date.
quests.explanation: "Since it began" introduces the outcome. The street party is an extra activity, not the change the question asks about.

quests.instruction: Read the text quickly and answer the question.
quests.passage: National parks ask hikers to stay on marked paths. Leaving the trail crushes plants, disturbs animals, and can create new paths that cause erosion. Rangers also ask visitors to carry out all litter, including apple cores, which take longer to disappear than most people think.
quests.question: What theme links the park's requests to hikers and visitors?
options: How hikers can protect the park
Which trails are the longest in the park
quests.correctAnswer: How hikers can protect the park
quests.hint: Group the two requests, staying on paths and carrying out litter. What do they share?
quests.explanation: Both rules aim to reduce harm to the park. The apple detail is an example, not the topic.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: A small mountain town used to depend on a single factory. When it closed, many young people left. The town then began promoting its trails and old buildings to tourists, and over five years, three new guesthouses and a bike shop have opened.
quests.question: What helped the town after the factory closed?
quests.correctAnswer: Attracting visitors
quests.hint: Look for the response the town made, after the bad news.
quests.explanation: Promotion of trails and old buildings led to guesthouses and a shop. The other options sound plausible but are never mentioned.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Some schools now use 3D printers in design lessons. Students draw an object on screen, watch the machine build it layer by layer, and then test whether it works. Teachers say the biggest benefit is that pupils learn from failed attempts, because a new version can be printed in an hour.
quests.question: What do teachers say is the biggest benefit?
options: Students can learn from their mistakes quickly
Students draw more neatly than before, on screen
The machines are cheap to run
quests.correctAnswer: Students can learn from their mistakes quickly
quests.hint: A superlative such as "biggest" signals the point the writer wants you to notice.
quests.explanation: Quick reprinting makes failure useful. The drawing and the layer-by-layer process describe how the lesson works.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Mobile banking has changed how people manage money. Customers can check balances, pay bills and send money in seconds, without visiting a branch. Yet banks warn that the convenience brings risks: fraudsters send fake messages that look official, so customers should never share passwords by text or email.
quests.question: What is the writer's main point?
options: Passwords should be changed every day by customers
Mobile banking is handy, but users must be careful
quests.correctAnswer: Mobile banking is handy, but users must be careful
quests.hint: A word like "yet" often signals the writer's real emphasis.
quests.explanation: The passage praises convenience and then warns about fraud. Closing branches is not mentioned, and no advice about changing passwords is given.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: The old public baths on Canal Street reopened in March after a three-year renovation. The main pool has been restored to its original blue tiles, and a modern gym has been added upstairs. Entry costs four dollars, and residents can buy a monthly pass for thirty.
quests.question: What was added during the renovation?
quests.correctAnswer: A modern gym
quests.hint: One thing was restored and another was added. Choose the second.
quests.explanation: The pool was restored, meaning it already existed. The gym was newly added upstairs.

quests.instruction: Read the text and answer the question.
quests.passage: Some trains have a quiet carriage where passengers are asked not to talk loudly, take phone calls or play music without headphones. Staff do not enforce the rule, so it depends on politeness. Most travellers respect it, and a gentle reminder is usually enough when someone forgets.
quests.question: How is the quiet-carriage rule mostly kept?
options: Through the good manners of passengers
By fines given out by the train staff on board
quests.correctAnswer: Through the good manners of passengers
quests.hint: Notice who does NOT enforce the rule, then find what does the job instead.
quests.explanation: Staff do not enforce it, so manners do the work. The passage gives no mention of fines, doors or tickets.

quests.instruction: Read the text quickly and answer the question.
quests.passage: Around one in five workers in some countries works at night, including nurses, bakers and bus drivers. Their bodies must adjust to sleeping in the daytime, which is not easy, and studies link long-term night work to health problems. Some employers now offer shorter shifts and quiet rest rooms to help staff recover.
quests.question: Which statement best summarises the passage?
options: Nurses and bakers are the most common night workers
Night work harms health, and some employers respond
quests.correctAnswer: Night work harms health, and some employers respond
quests.hint: A good summary includes the problem and the response, not a single example.
quests.explanation: The passage moves from the difficulty of night work to what some employers do. The job types are just examples.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: A community choir in the town of Alva began with six singers in a church hall. Today it has ninety members aged from seventeen to eighty-four, and rehearsals are held in a school. No audition is required; the conductor says enthusiasm matters more than a perfect voice.
quests.question: How has the choir changed since it began?
options: It has moved into a church
quests.correctAnswer: It has become much larger
quests.hint: Compare the beginning with the present. Time markers will guide you.
quests.explanation: Six singers became ninety. It began in a church hall and now rehearses in a school, so the church option reverses the facts.

quests.instruction: Read the passage, then choose the best answer.
quests.passage: Visitors to Kyoto in April often find the main sights crowded. Locals recommend starting at dawn, when temples are quiet and the light is soft, and leaving the busiest streets for late afternoon. Even a short walk away from the famous districts can reveal small gardens where you may be the only visitor.
quests.question: What advice do locals give?
options: See popular places early in the day
Stay only in the famous districts of the city
quests.correctAnswer: See popular places early in the day
quests.hint: Advice is often introduced by the word "recommend".
quests.explanation: Locals recommend dawn visits to avoid crowds. The passage does not tell visitors to skip April or to visit at night.
